name: Product Liability Directive
evidence_rating: ex-ante only: Commission forecasts, an evaluation of the old law and industry critique; applies from December 2026
summary: The Commission expected the new rules, which extend no-fault liability to software and make claims easier, to raise compensation for victims by up to tens of millions of euros a year, with a small rise in producers' insurance costs. The rules apply only to products placed on the market from December 2026, so there is no evidence yet; insurers warned of more litigation and harder-to-insure risks.

indicators.objective: The proposal's financial statement contains no indicators section; the memorandum only promises a review of application and transposition 6 years after entry into force

indicators.indicator: Annual compensation up EUR 0.15-22.13m (wider scope incl. software) and EUR 0.20-43.54m (easier burden of proof) compared with baseline
indicators.evidence: Not measured; Member States must apply the new rules to products placed on the market from 9 December 2026.

indicators.objective: Insurance and legal costs for producers
indicators.indicator: Insurance premiums up EUR 4.35-8.69m (scope) and EUR 14.35-28.71m (burden of proof) a year; legal costs up EUR 1.12-2.75m a year
indicators.evidence: Not measured. Insurers argued the reform would make some risks (psychological harm, data loss, cyber) hard to price and raise litigation and consumer costs.

indicators.indicator: Producers, including non-EU ones, encouraged to place only safe products; clear coverage of software and digital products

literature.citation: European Commission (2022), Impact Assessment accompanying the proposal for a Directive on liability for defective products (executive summary SWD(2022) 317), SWD(2022) 316
literature.title: Impact Assessment accompanying the proposal for a Directive on liability for defective products (executive summary SWD(2022) 317)
literature.outcomes: compensation to victims; insurance premiums; legal costs
literature.headline: Extending no-fault liability to software and other actors raises annual compensation by EUR 0.15-22.13m and easing the burden of proof by EUR 0.20-43.54m; premiums rise EUR 4.35-8.69m and EUR 14.35-28.71m a year; small unquantified price rises for non-EU products
literature.summary_plain: The Commission expected modest effects: tens of millions of euros a year more compensation for people harmed by defective products, including software, and a small rise in producers' insurance premiums.

literature.citation: European Commission (2018), Evaluation of Council Directive 85/374/EEC on liability for defective products, SWD(2018) 157
literature.title: Evaluation of Council Directive 85/374/EEC on liability for defective products
literature.method: ex-post evaluation (qualitative; cost-benefit analysis not possible for lack of data)
literature.outcomes: consumer protection; single market; burden of proof
literature.headline: The 1985 Directive contributes to consumer protection and a level playing field at reasonable cost, but the burden of proof, the EUR 500 threshold and unclear coverage of software and digital products limit its effectiveness
literature.summary_plain: The Commission's review of the 1985 law found it broadly worked but was hard for victims to use, especially for complex and digital products - the problems the new Directive targets.

literature.citation: Insurance Europe (2022), Key messages on the European Commission's proposal for a revision of the Product Liability Directive (PLD), Position paper, December 2022
literature.title: Key messages on the European Commission's proposal for a revision of the Product Liability Directive (PLD)
literature.headline: Proposal would compromise insurers' ability to price risk (psychological harm, data loss, cyber), increase litigation and ultimately consumer costs, and could harm innovation
literature.summary_plain: The insurance industry warned that the reform would make some risks hard to insure and lead to more lawsuits and higher costs.
literature.interested_party: Insurance industry federation; members underwrite product liability risk
